ci-cd-pipeline-architecture.core: A CI/CD pipeline is an automated assembly line: stages, jobs and steps structure the work, artifacts carry the built output forward (build once), caches speed up repeated inputs, and runners provide the compute.

first_principles.problem: Manual or monolithic delivery is slow, inconsistent and untraceable.

analogy.title: A modern factory
analogy.story: Production lines (stages), parallel workstations (jobs), a conveyor belt carrying the product (artifacts), a parts store (cache) and the machines (runners).
analogy.breaks: The factory itself needs maintenance and security; pipelines are production systems.

example.title: A well-architected pipeline

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A 12-minute, fully traceable path to production.

example.outcome: fast, repeatable, trustworthy delivery.

check.q: Why do parallel jobs need artifacts to share outputs?
check.a: Each job runs on a separate runner with its own filesystem.

build-systems-at-scale.core: At monorepo scale, builds must be hermetic (declared inputs only), therefore deterministic, so a dependency graph can rebuild only affected targets and remote caching and execution can share and parallelise the work across the organisation.

first_principles.problem: Full rebuilds take hours and differ between machines, which kills feedback loops.
truths: Same inputs should give the same outputs.
Work done once should be reused.

analogy.title: An industrial kitchen network
analogy.story: Sealed ingredient kits, identical recipes, cooking only changed dishes, a shared prepared-food freezer and a thousand cooks on call.
analogy.breaks: This is a significant investment, worth it at large scale but overkill for small repos.

example.title: One change, end to end

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Fast, correct feedback at any scale.

example.outcome: builds that scale with the organisation.

check.q: Which property must hold for any of the scaling techniques to work?
check.a: Hermeticity, which gives determinism.

deployment-strategies-blue-green-canary-.core: Zero-downtime deployment runs old and new versions side by side and controls traffic. Rolling replaces gradually, blue/green switches instantly, canary validates on a small real slice, and shadow mirrors traffic invisibly. Choose by risk, and automate with metric-gated controllers.

first_principles.problem: Maintenance windows and big-bang releases cause downtime and large blast radii.

analogy.title: Theatre understudies and previews
analogy.story: Replace cast members gradually (rolling), keep a full second cast ready (blue/green), run preview nights for small audiences (canary) and rehearse with a live audio feed (shadow).
analogy.breaks: Every strategy requires backward-compatible data and APIs during the overlap.

example.title: A high-risk payment service release

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A risky change ships with no user-visible incidents.

example.outcome: releases are routine, safe and reversible.

check.q: Which strategy gives instant rollback by flipping traffic back?
check.a: Blue/green.

gitops-pull-vs-push-secrets.core: GitOps makes Git the single source of truth: desired state is declared and reviewed in Git, in-cluster agents (ArgoCD, Flux) pull and reconcile continuously (self-healing drift), sync waves order dependencies, directories model environments, and secrets are encrypted or referenced, never plaintext.

first_principles.problem: Manual cluster edits and push-based pipelines with powerful credentials create unknown state and security risk.
truths: Declarative state can be versioned and reviewed.

analogy.title: A city run strictly from its official plans
analogy.story: Every change is filed in the plans first, inspectors constantly bring buildings back into line, construction follows phases, and vault codes are never posted publicly.
analogy.breaks: Break-glass procedures are still needed, and must be followed by committing the change back to Git.

example.title: A release in a GitOps shop
flow: CI builds image, opens PR bumping staging tag

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Every change is reviewed, audited and reversible with git revert.

example.outcome: deployments are declarative, secure and self-correcting.

check.q: How do you roll back a bad release in GitOps?
check.a: Revert the commit in Git, and the agent reconciles the cluster to the previous state.

progressive-delivery-feature-flags-aca.core: Progressive delivery separates deploy from release: flags give runtime control of feature exposure, canaries validate new versions on real traffic, automated canary analysis removes the human judgement bottleneck, and together they form a gated, reversible pipeline.

first_principles.problem: Big-bang releases expose every user to every bug at once.
truths: Exposure can be controlled independently of deployment.
Automated, statistical judgement is faster and fairer.

analogy.title: Opening a theme-park ride
analogy.story: Build it (deploy), test with staff (flag), open to a few guests (canary) with sensors (ACA), then open to all.
analogy.breaks: Flags and canaries need observability. Without metrics, progressive delivery is blind.

example.title: A complete rollout

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Zero user-facing incidents.

example.outcome: releases are gradual, measured and reversible.

check.q: What removes the human bottleneck in canary releases?
check.a: Automated canary analysis, which compares metrics statistically and decides promotion or rollback.

software-supply-chain-security-sbom-sigs.core: Trusting what you build requires layered evidence: SBOMs for what's inside, Grype scans for known flaws, signatures for who produced it (keyless with Sigstore), SLSA provenance for how, and verification of all of it before deploying.

first_principles.problem: Dependencies and build pipelines are prime attack targets, and unverifiable artifacts must be trusted blindly.
truths: Tampering can happen anywhere between build and run.

analogy.title: Pharmaceutical supply chain
analogy.story: Ingredient lists, contamination testing, sealed packaging, manufacturing records and pharmacist checks.
analogy.breaks: All of this proves integrity and origin, not that the code itself is benign.

example.title: A secured release pipeline

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Tampered, unsigned or unprovenanced images can't run.

example.outcome: every running artifact is verifiable.

check.q: Where should signatures and provenance be verified?
check.a: At deploy time, for example by a Kubernetes admission controller.

merge-queue-engineering.core: PR builds go stale as main moves, so green PRs can still break trunk. A merge queue tests each PR's exact combination with the latest main and the PRs ahead of it, with optimistic parallelism and batching for throughput and a consistent history style.

first_principles.problem: Broken trunks block whole teams despite every PR being green.
truths: Main changes after PR CI runs.

analogy.title: An airport runway controller
analogy.story: Planes land in order, each landing slot is verified clear, several approaches are managed at once, and the log is kept tidy.
analogy.breaks: Flaky tests undermine every queue strategy, so fix flakiness first.

example.title: A monorepo with 200 PRs a day

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A permanently green trunk at high throughput.

example.outcome: main stays green and teams stay unblocked.

check.q: What problem does a merge queue solve?
check.a: PRs that each pass CI but break main when combined, by testing the exact merge result before landing.

test-flakiness-reliability-tia.core: Flaky tests destroy trust in CI. Fight them by understanding root causes (timing, state, external dependencies, resources), quarantining with owners instead of blanket retries, running only impacted tests (TIA) and labelling failures as likely flaky or real from history.

first_principles.problem: When CI cries wolf, engineers stop listening, and real bugs ship.
truths: Running fewer relevant tests reduces noise.

analogy.title: Maintaining a reliable alarm system
analogy.story: Fix faulty sensors, isolate the noisy ones for repair, only arm the zones that matter, and check each alarm's history before panicking.
analogy.breaks: Flaky tests sometimes point to real concurrency bugs in production code.

example.title: A flaky-test programme

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A red build means something again.

example.outcome: CI that engineers trust.

check.q: Why do flaky tests ultimately let real bugs ship?
check.a: Engineers learn to ignore or re-run failures, so genuine regressions get dismissed as flakes.

artifact-management-oci-retention.core: Advanced artifact management treats the registry as a universal OCI warehouse: any artifact type, proxy caches for upstream resilience and policy, retention that keeps releases and expires noise, and signatures plus provenance so stored artifacts can be trusted.

first_principles.problem: Scattered artifacts, upstream outages, unbounded storage and unverifiable binaries.
truths: Everything a pipeline produces needs a home.

analogy.title: A modern logistics hub
analogy.story: Standard containers for every cargo type, a local depot buffering suppliers, scheduled clearance and tamper-evident seals.
analogy.breaks: The hub is a single point of failure, so it needs HA and replication.

example.title: A platform registry design

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Fast, resilient, affordable and trusted distribution.

example.outcome: artifacts are managed end to end.

check.q: Name two benefits of a proxy cache for public registries.
check.a: Resilience against upstream outages or deletions, and avoiding rate limits (plus a policy enforcement point).

pipeline-security-isolation-oidc-gvisor.core: Pipelines are privileged attack surface. Never run unverified remote scripts, isolate untrusted builds on ephemeral sandboxed runners with no secrets, replace static cloud keys with OIDC federation, and fetch scoped, short-lived secrets from a vault.

first_principles.problem: A single CI compromise (malicious PR, poisoned script, leaked key) gives attackers production access.

analogy.title: Securing a factory
analogy.story: Inspect deliveries (no curl|bash), quarantine unknown visitors (isolation), day badges instead of master keys (OIDC) and a locked safe (vault).
analogy.breaks: Security controls slow pipelines down a little, so automate them to keep friction low.

example.title: Hardening a deploy pipeline
flow: PR jobs on ephemeral runners, no secrets

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: There are no static keys anywhere, and untrusted code is contained.

example.outcome: a pipeline that's hard to weaponise.

check.q: What replaces long-lived cloud keys in modern CI?
check.a: OIDC federation, which exchanges a short-lived identity token for temporary scoped credentials.

release-orchestration-migrations-expand-.core: Release orchestration keeps every intermediate state compatible: avoid big bangs, treat database changes with care (versioned, online, roll-forward), use expand-contract for breaking changes, and run migrations once as gated Jobs.

first_principles.problem: Distributed releases fail when components and schemas change incompatibly at the same time.
truths: Data changes are hard to reverse.

analogy.title: Rebuilding a train station while trains keep running
analogy.story: New platforms open before old ones close, signals are updated in sequence, and one crew coordinates the switchover.
analogy.breaks: It's slower than a big bang, by design, and the safety is worth the time.

example.title: Splitting a 'name' field into first and last

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Zero downtime across 4 releases.

example.outcome: complex releases happen safely.

check.q: What are the three phases of expand-contract?
check.a: Expand (add new), migrate (dual-write, backfill, switch) and contract (remove old).

devex-ci-time-to-feedback-act.core: In CI, speed is safety. Measure time to feedback, keep the inner loop in seconds and the outer loop in minutes (fail fast, parallelise, cache), and make local runs predict CI with the same containers, thin YAML and tools like act.

first_principles.problem: Push-and-pray cycles waste hours, break focus and encourage risky batching.
truths: Early failures are the most valuable.

analogy.title: A responsive kitchen
analogy.story: Chefs taste as they cook (inner loop), the pass checks quickly before service (outer loop), and the practice kitchen matches the real one.
analogy.breaks: Don't trade away meaningful coverage for speed. Restructure, don't delete.

example.title: A DevEx improvement sprint
flow: make ci in same container locally

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Developers stay in flow.

example.outcome: fast, trustworthy feedback at every loop.

check.q: Which single metric best captures CI developer experience?
check.a: Time to feedback (especially time to the first failure).

ci-observability-opentelemetry.core: Pipelines are distributed systems and deserve production-grade observability. Use OpenTelemetry to trace runs, jobs and steps, decompose build time into queue, setup and execution, and build focused dashboards and alerts that drive action.

first_principles.problem: 'The build is slow' gets investigated by guesswork and log scrolling.

analogy.title: Air traffic operations
analogy.story: Every flight is tracked, delays are broken down by cause, and the control room shows only what operators need.
analogy.breaks: Observability costs money too, so sample and retain wisely.

example.title: A platform team's CI SLOs
flow: Regression found and fixed in a day

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: CI speed is managed like a product.

example.outcome: slow builds are diagnosed and fixed with data.

check.q: What's the first step when someone says 'the build is slow'?
check.a: Decompose total time into queue, setup and execution to find where the time actually goes.

ephemeral-environments-preview-stacks.core: Ephemeral environments replace the shared staging bottleneck with an isolated copy per PR. Git events drive create, update and destroy; seeding provides realistic but safe data; and TTLs, sweepers and scale-to-zero keep costs in check.

first_principles.problem: Shared staging serialises testing, mixes changes and slows delivery.
truths: Data and cost are the hard parts.

analogy.title: Pop-up shops
analogy.story: Each launches for a campaign, is stocked with sample goods, and closes automatically when the campaign ends.
analogy.breaks: Some integrations (third-party webhooks, OAuth callbacks) are hard to replicate per PR.

example.title: A complete preview platform
flow: Neon DB branch from anonymised seed

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Unlimited parallel staging at a small cost.

example.outcome: every change is tested in isolation before merging.

check.q: What are the two hardest parts of ephemeral environments?
check.a: Providing realistic, safe data and controlling cost (zombie environments).

github-actions-mastery-syntax-security.core: GitHub Actions is event-driven automation next to your code: workflows, jobs and steps, reuse through actions and reusable workflows, matrices for coverage, OIDC and environments for credentials, and hardening (SHA pins, minimal permissions, injection-safe inputs, ephemeral runners) for security.

first_principles.problem: Easy automation turns into copy-paste sprawl, credential leaks and supply-chain holes if it isn't designed deliberately.

analogy.title: A city transit system
analogy.story: Routes (workflows), shared bus designs (reusable workflows), parallel lines (matrix), passes instead of keys (OIDC) and security checks (hardening).
analogy.breaks: Deep platform coupling. Keep the logic in scripts for portability.

example.title: An organisation-wide CI standard

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Consistent, secure pipelines in every repo.

example.outcome: powerful automation that stays safe.

check.q: Name three GitHub Actions hardening practices.
check.a: Pin actions to SHAs, set minimal token permissions, and pass untrusted inputs via env vars rather than inline expressions.

database-ci-cd-liquibase-flyway-atlas.core: Database CI/CD respects data gravity: version every schema change, deliver breaking changes through expand-contract, apply them with migration-based (Flyway, Liquibase) or declarative (Atlas) tools, and recover by rolling code back and fixing forward rather than 'undoing' data.

first_principles.problem: Manual, big-bang schema changes cause drift, downtime and data loss.
truths: Old and new code overlap during deploys.

analogy.title: Renovating an occupied building
analogy.story: Plans are versioned, new rooms are built before old ones close, and you can't 'un-renovate', only renovate again.
analogy.breaks: Large data migrations still need special tooling (online schema change, batching).

example.title: A pipeline with schema changes
flow: CI: atlas lint + apply to ephemeral DB + tests

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Schema changes are as routine as code changes.

example.outcome: safe, automated database delivery.

check.q: What's the safest rollback strategy for a bad release with schema changes?
check.a: Keep the schema backward compatible, roll back only the code, then fix forward.

mobile-desktop-ci-cd-fastlane-mac-runner.core: Mobile and desktop CI/CD fight hardware and platform constraints: scarce macOS runners (licensing), mandatory code signing managed centrally, Fastlane to automate store releases, and device farms for real-hardware testing.

first_principles.problem: Container-centric CI patterns don't work for iOS and desktop apps.

analogy.title: Exporting goods to strict markets
analogy.story: Special factories (Mac runners), official certifications (signing), a customs broker (Fastlane) and real-world product testing (device farms).
analogy.breaks: Store review is still a manual gate you can't automate away.

example.title: An iOS release pipeline
flow: Main: Mac runner, match signing, build_app

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Push-button mobile releases.

example.outcome: mobile delivery as automated as backend delivery.

check.q: What are the two unique constraints of iOS CI compared with backend CI?
check.a: It requires macOS on Apple hardware, and every binary must be signed with Apple certificates and profiles.

dagger-ci-as-code.core: Dagger replaces YAML-bound pipelines with code: SDKs build container-operation DAGs that the BuildKit-based engine runs identically anywhere, with real programming constructs, automatic content-addressed caching and thin integration into any CI.

first_principles.problem: YAML pipelines are untestable locally, hard to make dynamic and locked to one vendor.
derivation: Run them on the **engine** locally and in CI.

analogy.title: Write once, run anywhere for pipelines
analogy.story: Like a portable app that runs on any computer the same way.
analogy.breaks: Adds an engine dependency and a learning curve, and simple pipelines may not need it.

example.title: A monorepo moves to Dagger
flow: CI time −40%, pipeline bugs fixed locally

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Pipelines become maintainable software.

example.outcome: CI pipelines with a real development workflow.

check.q: Does Dagger replace GitHub Actions or GitLab CI?
check.a: No. It runs inside them, handling pipeline logic while they handle triggers, secrets and runners.

tekton-kubernetes-native-pipelines.core: Tekton makes CI/CD a native part of Kubernetes: Tasks (Pods of step containers) and their runs, Pipelines composing Tasks into DAGs, workspaces sharing data through volumes, and Triggers turning webhooks into PipelineRuns. It scales with the cluster and is idle when unused.

first_principles.problem: Always-on CI servers are separate infrastructure that doesn't use Kubernetes' scheduling, RBAC and scaling.

analogy.title: An on-demand film studio
analogy.story: Sets (Pods) are built per scene, scheduled by the production plan (Pipeline), props are kept in shared storage (workspaces), and production starts when a script arrives (Triggers).
analogy.breaks: Verbose YAML and a low-level UX. Consider higher-level layers on top of it.

example.title: A complete Tekton CI
flow: PipelineRun: clone → test ∥ lint → kaniko build → deploy

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Kubernetes-native CI with no CI servers.

example.outcome: pipelines are Kubernetes objects.

check.q: What turns a Git webhook into a PipelineRun in Tekton?
check.a: Tekton Triggers: an EventListener with Interceptors, TriggerBindings and a TriggerTemplate.

environment-on-demand-terraform-helm.core: On-demand environments split infrastructure into a Terraform-managed foundation and Helm-deployed per-PR stacks, give each PR a wildcard-DNS HTTPS URL, clean up with events, TTLs and reconciliation, and surface the URL right in the PR.

first_principles.problem: A single shared QA environment serialises testing and causes collisions.
truths: Wildcard DNS and TLS make URLs instant.
Cleanup must not rely on events alone.

analogy.title: A mall with pop-up stalls
analogy.story: The mall is permanent, stalls open per campaign with their own sign, are listed in the directory, and are cleared when the campaign ends.
analogy.breaks: Stateful dependencies and third-party integrations remain the hard parts.

example.title: The full loop

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Unlimited parallel QA at controlled cost.

example.outcome: every change is testable in isolation, instantly.

check.q: Which layer does Terraform own in this architecture?
check.a: The long-lived foundation: network, cluster, DNS zone, wildcard certificate and shared services.
